O.outcome_detail: frequency of activity types in a systematic review of 126 K-12 ML activities

result.effect: Almost 60% of coded supervised-learning entries versus 2 activities

cells.quote: A systematic review of 126 K-12 ML activities, coded according to a taxonomy of algorithmic abstraction that ranges from invisible use to independent creation, confirms that supervised learning activities cluster overwhelmingly in the lowest abstraction levels: invisible use, button interaction, and model deployment together account for almost 60% of all coded supervised learning entries, while genuinely open-ended creation tasks appear only twice in the entire corpus [22].
cells.note: Descriptive distribution of activities, not a comparison of learner outcomes; the study text does not specify the review's synthesis design beyond calling it a systematic review.

cells.quote: Thematic coding reveals that GenAI tools are predominantly employed to support lesson planning, prompt generation, and creative ideation, and traditional AI tools are commonly used for designing analytics and for feedback design.

D.comparison: AI or GenAI as co-designer or dialogic partner

cells.quote: Teacher-AI collaboration in design manifests in multiple forms, with AI and GenAI most often serving as an assistant or content generator, and less frequently as a co-designer or dialogic partner.
cells.note: The direction indicates greater reported prevalence of assistant/content-generator roles; no numerical effect size is provided.

D.treatment: Teacher education and higher education contexts

O.outcome_detail: Distribution of educational contexts represented in the review

result.effect: 36.7% teacher education; 30.0% higher education; 20.0% secondary; 13.3% primary

cells.quote: Among the 28 studies included in the review, the majority were situated in teacher education (36.7%), re ﬂecting a strong research emphasis on how pre-service and in-service teachers engage with AI in instructional design contexts (indicated in Fig. 2). Another 30.0% of studies were set in general higher education contexts, focusing on university-level instructional design. Meanwhile, secondary education settings accounted for 20.0% of the sample, and primary education was the least represented (13.3%).
cells.note: This is a descriptive distributional contrast; the study does not report an inferential comparison or learning effect.

cells.quote: However, little attention is paid to the undesirable consequences of an indiscriminate and insufficiently thought-out application of AI, both in higher education and especially in K-12.
cells.note: The study reports a qualitative gap in the reviewed literature rather than an experimental comparison or measured effect.

D.treatment: AI learning experiences that assess learners’ understanding
D.comparison: AI learning experiences without reported outcome assessment

O.outcome_detail: understanding of AI concepts

cells.quote: There were hardly any experiences that assessed whether students understood AI concepts after the learning experience.
cells.note: The review reports an assessment gap rather than a comparative treatment effect; the treatment/comparison contrast is reconstructed from the reported presence versus absence of assessment.

O.outcome_detail: type of educational approach used to integrate AI literacy

cells.quote: By analyzing the data extracted, the papers were classified into two broad thematic categories according to the type of educational approach, namely, learning experience and theoretical perspective. The first category covers AI learning experiences focused on understanding a particular AI concept/technique or using specific tools/platforms to illustrate some AI concepts. The second category involves initiatives for the implementation of AI education for K-12 through the development of guidelines, curriculum design or teacher training, among others.
cells.note: The review reports a qualitative classification of approaches, not a comparative effect on learner outcomes; therefore no direction or effect size is reported.

O.outcome_detail: co-occurring science data-practice associations

cells.quote: "Notably, the results revealed distinct sets of co-occurring data practices in K–12 and higher education, with no overlapping association rules (i.e., no common combinations of practices) observed across the two categories."
cells.note: The quoted sentence is from the wiki entry rather than the supplied study-text excerpt; it reports the review's association analysis.

O.outcome_detail: emphasis on first-hand data and contextual, hands-on practices versus second-hand data analysis

cells.quote: "Higher education predominantly emphasized second-hand data analysis (e.g., using given data, applying statistics or computational methods, and selecting methods), while K–12 focused on first-hand data (i.e., producing their own data ) along with other data practices such as developing hypotheses, identifying variables , gathering information , making data-driven arguments , synthesizing results, and sharing results."
